messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kiet Phommasack is a forty-one-year-old Laotian-American contemporary dancer and choreographer who lives with his wife in Portland, Oregon. He presented for treatment with a PCL-5 score of 77, describing a presentation that had been quietly dismantling his life for the better part of two years. Before seeking help, he had told almost no one what had happened to him during a six-month deployment as a relief worker in a conflict zone in Southeast Asia, where he had been coordinating medical supply distribution in a region under intermittent shelling.

The incident that broke something in Kiet occurred in the late afternoon — around four o'clock — when a supply convoy he had helped organize was ambushed at a checkpoint. A vehicle ahead of his was struck and caught fire. Kiet pulled two colleagues from the wreckage, but a third man, a local driver named Boua, could not be reached in time. What Kiet remembers most viscerally is the smell: the acrid, suffocating stench of burning material and flesh, and the sharp reek of alcohol from a hand sanitizer container that had ruptured and soaked his sleeve as he worked. He remembers the angle of the late-afternoon light, amber and low, cutting through the smoke. He did not stay with Boua long enough. He has believed this ever since.

Back in Portland, Kiet returned to his dance company and attempted to resume teaching and rehearsing. For a time, the effort held. But the late afternoon began to betray him. Around four o'clock, something in the quality of the light — its warmth, its particular angle through the studio's high windows — would act as an immediate portal, collapsing the distance between Portland and the checkpoint entirely. The smell of something burning in a nearby restaurant kitchen, or the faint trace of alcohol from a dancer's injury spray, could produce the same effect without a moment's warning: the full scene would return, not as memory but as present reality, his body responding as though he were still there, crouching beside the burning vehicle, the heat against his face, Boua's voice gone silent. These intrusions did not feel like recollections. They felt like facts happening now.

What made the intrusions unbearable was not only their vividness but what they carried with them. Each time the memory broke through, it arrived wrapped in a wave of shame so acute it was almost physical — the certainty that he had failed Boua, that he had made a choice that revealed something irreparable about his character. This shame, in turn, deepened the memory's hold, giving it an emotional charge that kept it close to the surface. He found that when he sat with the appraisals — the conviction that he had violated everything he believed about who he was, that he had proven himself unreliable under the conditions that mattered most — the memories became more accessible, more easily triggered, as though his self-condemnation kept the neural pathways warm. The thought that he could not rely on himself, that his responses since the event had confirmed him as a lousy coper, seemed to prime him for the next intrusion; he would scan the studio for the smell of something burning, or tense at the afternoon light, already anticipating the collapse.

The loop had consequences his wife and colleagues could see even if they could not name it. He stopped scheduling rehearsals in the late afternoon, citing fatigue. He began keeping the studio windows covered. When a colleague used hand sanitizer near him during a warm-up, he left the room without explanation and did not return for an hour. His choreographic work, once fluid and collaborative, became halting. His wife noticed he flinched at the smell from their neighbor's fire pit on summer evenings, and that he had grown distant and self-critical in ways she did not recognize.

What finally brought Kiet to seek help was a performance he had to abandon mid-rehearsal when the smell of a candle the lighting designer had lit drifted across the stage at quarter past four on a Tuesday. He walked out, sat in his car, and wept. What he is most afraid of is that the shame is accurate — that what the memories keep showing him is simply true. What he is hoping, cautiously, is that someone might help him find out whether it is.
